title: Everywhere now
hook: Buddhist communities in Europe, Africa, Latin America and beyond
carry: a good man pervades every place

segments.voice: Yesterday, vipassana went west: rising, falling, hearing, thinking. Your line was insight travels. Did you note ten steps of walking? Day nine hundred fifty-two.

Three postcards. The first, from Brazil: a temple in São Paulo, incense, a family bowing before a Japanese altar, and a conversation in Portuguese afterward over tea. The second, from South Africa: a large temple with curved roofs on the grass near Pretoria, built by a Buddhist order from Taiwan. The third, from Germany: a quiet house on a hill on the northern edge of Berlin, with steps up to a shrine room, where monks from Sri Lanka live. Three continents, one teaching. Today, the end of a week of crossings, and a look at where the road has led.
screen: `A TEMPLE IN SÃO PAULO.` → `A TEMPLE NEAR PRETORIA.` → `A HOUSE IN BERLIN.`

segments.voice: First, families brought temples. When people move, their practice moves with them. Japanese families in Brazil built temples, just as they did in Hawaii and California. Sri Lankan, Thai, Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean and Tibetan communities have done the same in cities across Europe, the Americas, Africa and Australia, sometimes starting in a living room before there was a building. Second, seekers built centers. Others came to the teaching through books and travel. In Berlin, a doctor named Paul Dahlke built a house for Buddhist practice, and it still stands as a temple. Third, orders sent teachers. Some Asian orders built temples abroad on purpose. The Taiwanese order Fo Guang Shan built Nan Hua Temple in South Africa, near Pretoria, and from it monks and nuns have taught in other parts of Africa. Fourth, the week. Look at the road we've walked since the poem. The Light of Asia put the Buddha's life into English verse. In Chicago, the teaching spoke for itself. Zen came west in a cup of tea. Temples kept their practice going behind a fence. Tibetan teachers carried a tradition over the mountains. Insight came west as noting. And today, everywhere now. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words, compares the good to a scent that goes where flowers can't, and ends the verse like this: "a good man pervades every place." A teaching that began on foot in northern India now has shrine rooms on continents far from where it began.
screen: `FAMILIES BRING THEIR TEMPLES.` · `SEEKERS BUILD CENTERS.` · `ORDERS SEND TEACHERS.` · `A WEEK OF CROSSINGS.` · then, large: `EVERYWHERE NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a community far away. After the bell, if you like, look one up: a temple or sitting group in a country you've never been to. For now, picture one. Choose a place, any place far from where you're sitting. Picture a shrine room there, a small one, with a few people sitting, maybe at this very hour, in a language you don't speak. Breathe in, and know they're breathing too. Breathe out. Sit with them, across the distance. The bell holds the time.
Everywhere now. Temples in São Paulo, near Pretoria and in Berlin, built by families, seekers and orders, far from where the teaching began. Today's word.

Your line: a good man pervades every place. Today, when you pass a place of worship that isn't familiar, notice it, and remember someone there is practicing too. That's the week. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Buddhist communities around the world gather in temples, monasteries and meditation centers, from family temples of immigrant communities to centers founded by Western students and temples built abroad by Asian orders.

original.note: Pali sangha: the community of practice, now gathering far from where the teaching began.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism lives in Asia.
what it means: families, seekers and orders have planted temples in Europe, Africa, Latin America and beyond.
what a scholar hears: three routes at once: immigrant family temples, centers founded by converts, and temples built abroad by Asian orders like Fo Guang Shan.
